summary: LUNA-ASCENT is a beginner-friendly educational web game, built with Python and Flask, in which players design a simplified lunar orbiter mission. The player picks a mission objective (search for water ice, map the lunar surface, or study lunar minerals), a rocket (Pioneer, Pathfinder, or Atlas), an orbit (low, polar, or high lunar orbit), and a set of instruments (camera, mineral spectrometer, subsurface radar, and magnetometer). When the player clicks simulate, the app checks the design against four constraints: the spacecraft’s mass must fit the rocket’s capacity, the total cost must stay within the budget of 120, the power needed must not exceed 100, and the data produced must fit what the chosen orbit can transmit. Each rule passed earns 25 points, and a design that passes all four also gets a bonus based on its science value, for a maximum score of 100, then is labeled Mission Ready, Mission at Risk, or Mission Not Ready, with a list of issues to fix. The project teaches that real space missions are about balancing trade-offs, since more capable instruments bring more science but also add cost, weight, power demand, and data. The code is stored on GitHub and hosted online through Render using gunicorn, and all numbers are simplified game-balance values rather than real NASA specifications.
details:
LUNA-ASCENT is an educational web game in which the player designs a simplified lunar orbiter mission and tests whether the design would work. It is built with Python and Flask for the backend logic, an HTML/CSS/JavaScript page (templates/index.html) for the interface, and gunicorn as the production server. The code is stored on GitHub and hosted online through Render. The player picks a mission objective (search for water ice, map the lunar surface, or study lunar minerals), a rocket (Pioneer with capacity 180, Pathfinder with 300, or Atlas with 500), an orbit (low, polar, or high lunar orbit), and any combination of four instruments: a high-resolution camera, a mineral spectrometer, a subsurface radar, and a magnetometer. Each instrument has its own mass, power use, cost, data output, and science value, so a more capable instrument such as the radar brings more science but also costs more and weighs more. It also needs more power and produces more data. When the player clicks simulate, the browser sends the choices as JSON to the /simulate route. The server falls back to default choices (ice objective, Pioneer rocket, low orbit) if something is missing or unknown, and it returns an error if the data is invalid.

The backend then adds up the totals: mass starts at 80 plus the instruments, power needed starts at 25 plus the instruments, and cost starts at 30 plus the rocket, the orbit, and the instruments. It also adds up the data generated and the science value, which is the objective bonus plus the instrument science. These totals are checked against four rules: the mass must fit the rocket’s capacity, the cost must stay within a budget of 120, the power needed must not exceed the 100 available, and the data produced must fit the orbit’s communications limit (70 for low, 60 for polar, 85 for high). Each rule passed earns 25 points. The mission is labeled Mission Ready with no problems, Mission at Risk with one problem, and Mission Not Ready with two or more, and the page shows the totals along with a plain-language list of issues to fix. For example, a Pioneer rocket in low lunar orbit carrying the camera and the spectrometer has a mass of 175 out of 180, a cost of 95 out of 120, a power need of 75 out of 100, and 60 units of data against a limit of 70. It passes all four rules and has a science value of 90 for the ice objective. Using all four instruments always fails the power rule (130 needed against 100 available), which gives the game a built-in challenge.

The project teaches that real space missions are about balancing trade-offs rather than maximizing any single feature, and all numbers are simplified game-balance values, not real NASA specifications. The code has some points that would make good future improvements. The science bonus currently has no effect on the score, because the four rules already add up to 100, so making each rule worth 20 points and letting science add up to 20 more would fix that. The orbit’s coverage value is calculated but never used, the objectives don’t reward matching instruments (radar isn’t favored for the ice objective, for example), and a mission with no instruments still passes every rule and shows Mission Ready. The idea behind the game is to let students and beginners experience, in a few minutes, the kind of compromises that real mission designers face. It was created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, whose theme is The lunar ascent, and the Moon was chosen as the setting because it is the next destination in human space exploration, with water ice, surface mapping, and mineral studies being real scientific goals of lunar missions. Instead of reading about engineering constraints, the player feels them: a design that looks exciting on paper can fail because the rocket is too small, the budget is too tight, or the spacecraft cannot send its data back to Earth. The game does not require any prior knowledge of space science, and the plain-language feedback after every simulation explains what went wrong, so players can learn by trying again.

The choices are designed so that no option is best in every situation. The Pioneer rocket is the cheapest at a cost of 25 but can carry only 180 units of mass, so after the spacecraft’s base mass of 80 it leaves room for just 100 units of instruments. The Atlas rocket can carry 500 but costs 60, which uses up half of the 120 budget on its own once the base cost of 30 is added. The orbits work the same way. Polar lunar orbit gives the best surface coverage (95) but the lowest communications limit (60) and the highest cost (15), high lunar orbit is the cheapest (8) and has the best communications limit (85) but the weakest coverage (55), and low lunar orbit sits in between with a communications limit of 70 and coverage of 65. A player who wants to carry more instruments therefore has to think about the rocket, the orbit, the power, and the budget at the same time.

The project has some limitations, and being open about them is part of its educational value. The values are made up for game balance, so the game cannot be used to plan or evaluate a real mission. The simulation checks only four constraints and does not model things like launch windows, fuel, orbit mechanics, radiation, temperature, or how long the mission lasts

Tools used- Python, Flask, Github, Render
